extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of political theory, constitutional law, and comparative government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains normative and descriptive criteria about central vs. local administration, effects of centralization, and the defining characteristics and limits of judicial power in the United States as presented in a political-theory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between central government and central administration
rubrics_metrics.description: When the power which directs the general interests is centred ... it constitutes a central government. ... the power of directing partial or local interests, when brought together into one place, constitutes what may be termed a central administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text defines two kinds of centralization (political/legislative centralization directing general interests, and administrative centralization directing local/partial interests), notes that they sometimes coalesce but are separable, and that classifying the objects each governs helps distinguish them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of combining central government with administrative centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: A central government acquires immense power when united to administrative centralization; it accustoms men to set their own will habitually and completely aside, submitting in every respect and at all times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combined centralization not only compels obedience but shapes habits and weakens public spirit: it may secure transient victories or greatness but 'it cannot ensure the durable prosperity of a nation.' Example: Louis XIV's France—complete central government with less centralized administration than modern states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization produces routine regularity but undermines civic initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralization imparts an admirable regularity to the routine of business ... it excels more in prevention than in action. Its force deserts it when society is to be disturbed or accelerated in its course; and if once the co‑operation of private citizens is necessary ... the secret of its impotence is disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central administrations are effective at uniformity, petty police, and stable routine, creating 'drowsy precision' and prevention, but they struggle to mobilize free, responsible citizen action or to adapt rapidly when popular cooperation is required. China is offered as an example of order without improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits of local administration for civic energy and public welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: The collective strength of the citizens will always conduce more efficaciously to the public welfare than the authority of the Government when the people is enlightened and awake to its interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local institutions promote engagement: citizens undertake public works, establish schools and places of worship, maintain roads, and assist in crime detection/prosecution. The American examples show private undertakings often exceed what government could do, and citizen participation reduces crime elusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and limits of excessive local autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Local authority has been carried to lengths which no European nation could endure without great inconvenience ... This method of collecting taxes is slow as well as inconvenient, and it would prove a perpetual hindrance to a Government whose pecuniary demands were large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive decentralization leads to lack of uniform regulations, slow and inconvenient administration (tax collection, police oversight), neglect of undertakings needing continuous attention, and difficulty executing projects of national scope because no national administration directs them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government officers for matters materially affecting state existence should be centrally appointed and removable
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable that, in whatever materially affects its existence, the Government should be served by officers of its own, appointed by itself, removable at pleasure, and accustomed to rapid methods of proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For functions that critically affect state survival or urgent national needs, centralized appointment and removable officers enable quicker, more efficacious action than relying solely on local elected or temporary agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central authority ought to retain inspection/supervision over local administration
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority which represents the State ought not, I think, to waive the right of inspecting the local administration, even when it does not interfere more actively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A limited system of central oversight (for example, a government agent prosecuting town/county misdemeanors) could produce more uniform order without compromising township independence. The text argues for inspection rights short of active interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local administration should not be supplanted by central administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a central administration affects to supersede the persons most interested, I am inclined to suppose that it is either misled or desirous to mislead. ... it cannot of itself embrace all the details of the existence of a great nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central administrations should avoid displacing local actors who have primary interest and knowledge; attempting to manage all details leads to imperfect results or self-exhaustion. Local actors need freedom and responsibility to secure their cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provincial institutions are indispensable in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: I believe that provincial institutions are useful to all nations, but nowhere do they appear to me to be more indispensable than amongst a democratic people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provincial/local institutions train citizens in self-government, provide resistance to tyranny, and teach the exercise of freedom in small concerns so it can be used temperately in greater affairs. Democracies lacking provincial institutions risk impotence and vulnerability to central despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracies have a tendency toward political centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic nations are most exposed to fall beneath the yoke of a central administration ... The constant tendency of these nations is to concentrate all the strength of the Government in the hands of the only power which directly represents the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because in democracies the people appear as a mass of equal individuals, the representative body that speaks for them tends to appropriate other powers and penetrate administration, risking legislative encroachment and centralization (historical example: post-Revolutionary France).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial power characteristic — duty of arbitration (case-based decision-making)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first characteristic of judicial power in all nations is the duty of arbitration. But rights must be contested in order to warrant the interference of a tribunal; and an action must be brought to obtain the decision of a judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges decide disputes brought before them; they are not initiators of legal inquiries. When a judge in a case attacks a law, he stays within duties because deciding the case requires law interpretation; but acting without a case would invade legislative domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial power characteristic — pronouncing on special cases, not abstract general principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The second characteristic ... is that it pronounces on special cases, and not upon general principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judge may, in deciding a particular case, produce effects that undermine a general principle, but directly attacking a general principle without a concrete case exceeds the ordinary judicial function and becomes a political act rather than judicial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial power characteristic — passive/inactive until appealed to
rubrics_metrics.description: The third characteristic ... is its inability to act unless it is appealed to, or until it has taken cognizance of an affair. The judicial power is by its nature devoid of action; it must be put in motion in order to produce a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts do not pursue criminals or open investigations on their own motion; a judge who opens proceedings or usurps censorship would violate the passive nature of the judiciary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis and scope of American judicial review (right to refuse to apply unconstitutional laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Americans have acknowledged the right of the judges to found their decisions on the constitution rather than on the laws. In other words, they have left them at liberty not to apply such laws as may appear to them to be unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike other countries where courts' claims to such a right failed, in the U.S. judicial review is recognized and uncontroverted because the Constitution is treated as the first law, binding on legislator and citizen, and not modifiable by ordinary legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification and limits of judicial review depend on constitutional system
rubrics_metrics.description: If in France the tribunals were authorized to disobey the laws on the ground of their being opposed to the constitution, the supreme power would in fact be placed in their hands ... In England the Parliament which makes the laws also makes the constitution ... But neither of these remarks is applicable to America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legitimacy and risk of judicial review differ: in France (constitution viewed as immutable) or England (Parliamentary sovereignty) judicial nullification of laws would be problematic; in the U.S., because the constitution is supreme but amendable by the people under prescribed rules, judicial review is justified and less dangerous—but the text notes the balance depends on how constitutional amendment and sovereignty are structured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should connect patriotism to daily life to rekindle civic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws cannot succeed in rekindling the ardor of an extinguished faith, but men may be interested in the fate of their country by the laws. By this influence the vague impulse of patriotism ... may be directed and revived; and if it be connected with the thoughts, the passions, and the daily habits of life, it may be consolidated into a durable and rational sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and institutional design that ties national concerns to everyday civic habits can help convert diffuse patriotism into sustained civic virtue; the law can be an instrument to revive and channel public sentiment into responsible collective action.
